analysis.one_liner: Lets workers sue and win real damages when employers punish union activity, and imposes penalties on violators.
analysis.headline: The bill won 32 Senate sponsors but never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The WAGE Act would have rewritten the National Labor Relations Act, the 1935 law protecting workers' right to organize. It would have let workers sue employers in court and collect double back pay when fired for union activity, imposed civil fines of up to $100,000 on repeat violators, made union-organizing orders self-enforcing, extended protections to workers misclassified as supervisors or contractors, and required binding arbitration when employers stall first contracts. It was introduced by Senator Patty Murray with 31 cosponsors and referred to the Senate labor committee, which took no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who try to organize unions or speak up about pay and conditions, especially those fired or punished for it; today they must rely on the National Labor Relations Board, and even a win often means only back pay after years of delay. Under this bill, they could also go to federal court, collect doubled back pay with no deductions, and employers could face fines up to $100,000 per violation, with personal liability for executives who direct the violations. Workers wrongly labeled supervisors or independent contractors would gain NLRA coverage, and the bill would bar denying back pay to unauthorized immigrants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers organizing unions or punished for it

how_it_helps.text: Doubles back pay for workers fired or otherwise harmed by unfair labor practices, with no reduction for interim earnings, and adds civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders [S2][S3].

Creates a private right of action letting workers sue employers in federal court for certain violations, with relief modeled on Civil Rights Act remedies and possible attorney's fees, instead of relying solely on the NLRB to prosecute [S2][S3].

Makes NLRB orders self-enforcing, with a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation for disobedience, ending the current requirement that the Board petition a court before its orders take effect [S2][S3].

Requires the NLRB to order collective bargaining whenever a majority of votes cast favor union representation, and to order bargaining rather than a rerun election when employer interference tainted a fair vote [S2][S3].
Extends NLRA protections to workers misclassified as independent contractors (using a three-part test) and narrows the definition of supervisor so more employees are covered [S2][S3].
Sets a timed process for first contracts: bargaining within 10 days, mediation after 90 days, and binding arbitration before a tripartite panel if mediation fails, lasting two years [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face civil penalties up to $100,000 per serious violation, doubled back-pay awards, director and officer liability, joint and several liability when using staffing-agency workers, and mandatory arbitration of first-contract disputes. The AFL-CIO-backed approach of the bill reflects union priorities; employers' groups opposed similar legislation, though no opposition appears in the congressional record for this bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing organizing drives and their executives

drawbacks.text: The penalty regime is steep by design: civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation for repeat offenders, doubled back pay with no offsets, and personal liability for directors and officers, which small employers could find disproportionate [S3].

Binding arbitration of first-contract disputes would let a three-person panel impose a two-year contract without either side's agreement, overriding the NLRA's traditional preference for voluntary bargaining [S3].

The three-part independent-contractor test is strict enough that some genuinely self-employed workers could be reclassified as employees for NLRA purposes, affecting businesses that rely on contract labor [S3].

Making NLRB orders self-enforcing and limiting court review of Board fact-finding shifts power from courts to the agency, which critics of the Board's composition would object to on due-process grounds [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and documented gap: the findings cite that one in three organizing campaigns involves illegal firings, FY2014 reinstatement orders for 3,240 workers, and remedies far weaker than under the Civil Rights Act [S3]. The costs fall on employers and are the point — deterrence — but the mandatory-arbitration mechanism for first contracts and the aggressive contractor test would genuinely remove bargaining flexibility and are the strongest fair objections. The bill's core remedies closely mirror those other employment laws already use, which tempers the severity argument.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the WAGE Act on November 16, 2017, with 17 original cosponsors including Senators Brown, Sanders, Sanders-aligned progressives, and moderates like Carper and Coons [S3].
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, the standard first step [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors in total — 30 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republicans [S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the bill's record: no hearings, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote [S1][S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced doubled damages, civil penalties, and joint liability avoided the stricter regime, since the bill died without a committee markup or vote. Workers trying to organize unions remain under the weaker pre-existing remedies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers; workers kept the weaker status quo

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican joined.

against.name: Senate Republicans (majority in the 115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Brought no labor-law-strengthening legislation to the floor during the Congress; the bill had no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Senator Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Senate committee took no action.

industries.industry: Employers facing union organizing drives (retail, hospitality, manufacturing, logistics)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed them to doubled back-pay awards, civil fines up to $100,000 per violation, and fast-track injunctions when they fire or retaliate against workers who organize — the very conduct the bill was written to deter. Its death leaves their current penalty structure in place.

A strict three-part test would have denied independent-contractor status to many workers, extending union and NLRA protections into sectors built on contractor classification. The bill never advanced, so existing classification rules stand.
Joint and several liability would have made client employers directly liable for violations involving supplied workers, shrinking a key protective arrangement in the temp-staffing business model.

Bargaining orders on majority votes, mandatory arbitration of first contracts, and tougher remedies would have made organizing more likely to succeed and union contracts more durable. The bill's demise preserves the harder organizing environment unions describe in its findings.
